facts: Microbiologists noticed odd repeating DNA sequences in bacteria and other microbes, at first with no known use.
Francisco Mojica in Spain, working on microbes from salt marshes, worked out that these sequences were part of a defence system against viruses.
Bacteria store bits of virus DNA and use them to recognise and cut the same virus later.
Jennifer Doudna and Emmanuelle Charpentier met at a conference in Puerto Rico in 2011 and joined forces.
In 2012 they showed the bacterial enzyme Cas9, guided by RNA, could be told which spot of DNA to cut.
They shared the 2020 Nobel Prize in Chemistry.

conversation_variants.thirty_sec_idea: Microbiologists noticed strange repeating DNA in bacteria and could not say what it was for. It turned out to be a defence system: bacteria store bits of virus DNA and use them to find and cut the same virus later. In 2012 Jennifer Doudna and Emmanuelle Charpentier showed this could be steered to cut a chosen spot in DNA. They shared the 2020 Nobel Prize. Walter Isaacson tells it in The Code Breaker.
